title: New project
idea: A platform for live local music: bands find venues to play, venues find bands for their quiet nights, and fans buy tickets and discover shows.

data.industry: Live music, event discovery, and venue booking marketplace
data.idea_summary: A platform for live local music that helps bands find venues to perform, helps venues book bands for quieter nights, and enables fans to discover shows and buy tickets.
customer_segment_candidates: Local bands and independent musicians seeking performance opportunities
Music venues seeking live acts to fill quieter nights
Local live-music fans seeking show discovery and ticket purchasing

Her band is early-stage: it has released music online, plays occasional local shows, and is trying to build a reliable regional audience.

data.situation_narrative: On a Tuesday evening after her café shift, Maya opens the platform on her phone to find a paid local date for her four-piece indie-pop band next month. She filters venue requests by weekday availability, genre fit, capacity, backline, and minimum guarantee, then finds a brewery seeking an upbeat act for a quiet Thursday. Its verified profile shows a 90-person room, a usable PA, a 45-minute set, a fixed fee plus a clearly defined ticket split, and promotion and cancellation terms. Maya sends the band’s saved performance profile, including live footage, EPK, technical needs, and the dates already confirmed by her bandmates. The venue manager accepts through the platform, and both sides confirm the set time, payment schedule, ticket allocation, and promotional responsibilities in one booking record. Maya shares the platform ticket link with the band’s followers and, after the show, uses attendee follow options to invite new listeners to the next date. The value of this booking depends on participating venues offering live slots, while the platform can also connect the resulting show to fans buying tickets.

data.situation_narrative: On a Monday morning, Marcus sees that the venue has no programming for the following Thursday, a night that is usually too quiet to justify a full staff shift. Instead of sorting through old emails and social-media messages, he uses the platform to filter verified local bands by genre, Thursday availability, audience size, past attendance at similar-capacity rooms, technical needs, and cancellation record. He shortlists a soul-funk trio whose live video suits the venue and whose profile shows dependable local references and a realistic draw for a weeknight. Through the platform, Marcus proposes an early show with a modest door split, specifies the house backline and set times, and assigns promotion tasks to both parties. Once the band accepts the terms, the date is confirmed and a ticket page is automatically published for local fans. During the week, Marcus checks ticket sales and uses the shared promotion checklist rather than chasing messages across channels. He staffs the night conservatively, then reviews ticket scans, bar spend, and attendance after the show to decide whether to rebook the trio and which similar acts could help make future Thursdays profitable.

data.situation_narrative: On a Tuesday lunchtime, Maya is deciding whether she has enough energy for a social plan after work on Thursday. Instead of checking several venue calendars and Instagram stories, she opens the platform’s local feed on her phone. It highlights a nearby independent venue’s quieter-night show: an indie-soul headliner she has not heard before, a short live clip, genre tags, two support acts, verified set times, accessibility details, and a clear total ticket price of $14 including fees. A recommendation notes that two friends with similar saved artists follow the headliner. Maya listens to the clips, checks that the venue is a short transit ride from her apartment, and shares the event in her group chat with a built-in ticket link. When two friends agree, she buys three mobile tickets in one checkout, receives immediate confirmation and calendar reminders, and feels confident the listing is current because the venue and artists are verified. On Thursday, the tickets are scanned at the door; after discovering a standout support act, Maya posts a short video and saves the artist to receive future show alerts.

epicenter.rationale: The strongest signal is customer-driven: Maya has a clearly expressed unmet need for a reliable, professional way to find suitable gigs, evaluate venues, secure transparent terms, and build a dependable flow of paid performances. The proposed platform directly addresses these pains and gains through venue discovery, booking, and fan conversion. It is also finance-driven because ticket sales through the platform are explicitly identified as the monetization mechanism, making transaction revenue a stated part of the concept. No existing resource, infrastructure, or partnership is provided, and the brief does not primarily frame the idea as a radically new offer that requires rebuilding every other business-model component.

What if every live-music booking had to function like a transparent, standardized agreement before either side committed—covering set length, compensation, ticket allocation, promotional duties, equipment, and cancellation terms?
What if venues had to share the financial downside of weak attendance or cancellation instead of leaving independent bands to absorb travel, rehearsal, and opportunity costs?
What if ticket buyers discovered local artists first and chose venues second, forcing venues to compete for artists with fairer terms and better working conditions?

epicenter.rationale: The concept responds directly to Marcus's pronounced unmet needs: filling quiet midweek nights, reducing fragmented booking administration, finding dependable local acts, and converting discovery into reliable attendance and bar revenue. It is also finance-driven because the brief explicitly identifies ticket sales through the platform as monetization, while the venue persona is strongly motivated by profitable events, predictable revenue, and lower losses from lightly attended nights. No existing resource, infrastructure, or partnership is identified, and the platform concept does not clearly establish a wholly new value proposition that requires the business model to be rebuilt beyond the marketplace itself.

data.narrative_text:
On Tuesday evening after her café shift, Maya Torres needs a paid local date next month for her four-piece indie-pop band. Finding one normally means chasing scattered posts, unanswered messages, and informal contacts. Even when a venue responds, she may not know whether its room, audience, equipment, pay, or ticket expectations justify coordinating four musicians’ day jobs, rehearsals, and transport.

She opens the mobile marketplace and filters active venue opportunities by weekday availability, indie-pop fit, capacity, backline, and minimum terms. A brewery’s quiet Thursday slot appears with a verified profile: a 90-person room, usable PA, a 45-minute set, a fixed fee, a defined ticket split, and stated promotion and cancellation terms.

Maya sends her saved profile rather than rebuilding a pitch. It includes the band’s live footage, technical needs, availability, and past-show information. The venue accepts, and a standardized booking record makes the set time, payment, ticket allocation, equipment, promotion duties, and cancellation handling visible to both sides. Shared checklists reduce the risk that either party misses a commitment; completed-gig reviews give Maya a basis for trusting the venue and, after the show, strengthen her own reliability record.

The confirmed booking generates a ticket page. Maya shares its link with followers and through group chats, while fans see current show details and an all-in mobile ticket price. Ticket confirmations, reminders, and event-change alerts make attendance easier; ticket scans and attendance records also give the venue and band a clearer view of the night’s result.

Maya pays no vague administrative cost for this clarity; the platform earns a transaction fee when her band-venue booking is confirmed. It also earns venue-plan or completed-booking fees for discovery and administration, plus transparent ticket service and transaction fees on tickets sold. The model depends on verified venue slots, band profiles and live media, and trust data, supported by payment and ticket-scanning partners. Its ongoing work is to activate local supply and demand, match fit and availability, operate booking and entry, and handle verification, updates, refunds, and disputes.

data.hook: After a café shift, Maya needs a paid date for her indie-pop band—not another night of chasing scattered posts, unanswered messages, and unclear venue terms. She needs to know that the room, equipment, pay, ticket expectations, and cancellation terms work before coordinating four musicians’ schedules.
risk_analysis: Bands and venues may continue arranging shows through direct outreach, personal networks, social media, and informal promotion rather than using the platform. The response is to make the workflow meaningfully clearer than informal coordination through verified opportunities, saved artist profiles, standardized terms, shared checklists, reviews, and integrated ticketing.

Fees may face pressure from competing booking, discovery, and ticketing services that offer lower prices, broader inventory, or simpler workflows. The platform addresses this through an integrated value proposition: fit- and availability-based matching, transparent booking administration, trusted show information, and low-cost transparent ticket fees.

Margins may be constrained because booking and ticket fees must cover payment processing, refunds, support, trust-and-safety, and marketplace activation. Transparent fee design and multiple revenue streams—booking fees, venue plans or completed-booking fees, and ticketing fees—help align revenue with transaction activity, while the operating model must manage processing, refund, and support costs closely.

Costs could grow ahead of transaction revenue while the platform recruits venues, bands, and fans and operates verification, dispute handling, ticketing, and entry infrastructure. The model focuses activation in a launch geography and uses self-service profiles, filters, applications, and booking workflows to support scalable participation.

Inaccurate profiles, technical requirements, availability, event details, or reviews could weaken matching and trust. The platform mitigates this through profile verification, moderation of reviews, standardized booking terms, visible responsibilities and changes, and ongoing maintenance of reliable event information.

Failures in booking, ticketing, refunds, event updates, or mobile entry would directly disrupt scheduled events and damage trust. The platform depends on ticketing, mobile-entry, event-update infrastructure and payment and ticket-scanning partners, alongside in-app support and dispute handling for cancellations, late payments, and unclear terms.

The model depends materially on independent venues for bookable quiet-night inventory and on payment and ticket-scanning providers for checkout, payouts, and entry. It mitigates this dependency by building relationships with independent venues, artist communities, and local discovery partners, while maintaining operational focus on accurate slot information and reliable transaction workflows.

Cancellations, late payments, poor matching, disappointing promotion, or unreliable event information could cause bands, venues, and fans to leave and could damage relationships across the marketplace. Clear cancellation and payment terms, shared promotion and booking checklists, mutual completed-gig reviews, alerts for changes, and dispute handling are designed to make responsibilities visible and resolve issues consistently.
data.business_model_summary: The platform gives early-stage independent bands verified, well-matched paid performance opportunities; helps independent venue managers program underused weeknight capacity with vetted acts; and gives urban local-music fans trustworthy show discovery and all-in mobile ticketing. Bands and venues use a mobile marketplace to match on genre, availability, technical requirements, capacity, and minimum terms, then confirm through standardized booking records and shared checklists. Fans discover shows through a personalized local feed, shareable event links, and reminders, and buy tickets through mobile checkout and entry. Revenue comes from booking transaction fees, venue plans or completed-booking fees, and transparent ticket service and transaction fees. The model relies on verified venue slots and band profiles, trust and attendance data, booking and ticketing workflows, and payment and ticket-scanning partners.
competitive_advantages: A multi-sided platform advantage: bands, venues, and fans reinforce one another. Better venue inventory creates more relevant opportunities for bands; confirmed shows create inventory for fans; and ticket sales and attendance signals help venues and bands assess results.

Standardized booking records replace informal, fragmented arrangements with explicit terms for set time, pay, ticket allocation, equipment, promotion responsibilities, and cancellations—reducing ambiguity before a booking is accepted.

Trust is built into the operating workflow through verified profiles, completed-gig reviews, venue references, reliability records, and shared checklists, rather than relying solely on informal local contacts.

The model combines venue booking, current event information, all-in mobile ticketing, ticket scanning, and attendance records in one local-show journey, linking booking quality to fan experience and post-show performance signals.
